sentences.text: Ahshislepelta is a dinosaur belonging to the class Ornithischia, specifically within the family Ankylosauridae.
The genus name combines the locality name Ah-shi-sle-pah Wash with the Greek word peltè, meaning shield.
The species name minor means 'small' in Latin, reflecting its modest adult size compared to other North American ankylosaurids.
A unique derived feature distinguishes this animal: a projection on the scapula where the acromial process forms an overhang equal to one-quarter of the scapula's width.
Unlike most other ankylosaurids except Euoplocephalus, Ahshislepelta possesses osteoderms with a uniformly pitted texture and sparse neurovascular grooves.
The left humerus is massive, measuring 31 cm in length, with a well-developed deltopectoral crest that reaches 15 cm at its widest point.
The largest osteoderm found in the thoracic region measures 15 cm long, 12 cm wide, and 10 cm high, while the smallest associated ossicle has a diameter of only 1 cm.
The coracoid bone is approximately 16 cm long with the foramen located anterodorsal to the glenoid cavity, and the scapula and coracoid were firmly fused into an escapulocoracoid.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as SMP VP-1930, includes a partial girdle, vertebrae fragments, thoracic osteoderms, and other postcranial parts of an adult.
Based on humerus size, Ahshislepelta was larger than Eopinacosaurus but smaller than Talarurus and Pinacosaurus grangeri.
Researchers identified a unique derived feature: a projection on the scapula where the acromial process forms an overhang equal to one-quarter of the scapula's width.
Unlike other ankylosaurids except Euoplocephalus, Ahshislepelta has osteoderms with uniformly pitted texture and sparse neurovascular grooves.
Ahshislepelta was named in 2011 by paleontologists Michael Burns and Robert M. Sullivan, with the type species being Ahshislepelta minor.
A partial skeleton was discovered in 2005 at the Ah-shi-sle-pah Wilderness Study Area in New Mexico, collected from the Hunter Wash Member of the Kirtland Formation in the San Juan Basin.
The holotype specimen was collected during field seasons between 2005 and 2009 before being formally described in 2011.
The scapula and coracoid were firmly fused into an escapulocoracoid, indicating that the specimen was not a juvenile.
Burns and Sullivan originally classified Ahshislepelta as an ankylosaurid within Ankylosaurinae, though this was not based on phylogenetic analysis.
Several studies have favored classifying Ahshislepelta as a nodosaurid rather than an ankylosaurid.
Ahshislepelta lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage, in the Hunter Wash Member of the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico.
Evidence suggests the environment where Ahshislepelta lived had a warm temperate to subtropical climate.
Ahshislepelta coexisted with Stegoceras, Navajoceratops, Terminocavus, Ziapelta, Bistahieversor, and Navajodactylus.
It is debated whether Ahshislepelta belongs to Ankylosauridae or Nodosauridae, with some analyses supporting Ankylosauridae and others supporting Nodosauridae.
